01-why

Every AI call is a bill for three choices: which model, how hard it thinks, and how many words go in and out. Good Enough makes all three as cheap as they can be, without losing quality, using NVIDIA Nemmo-tron models on Neb-ee-us Token Factory.
02-problem
The catch is what we call the answer-key problem. To prove a cheaper setup is good enough, it sounds like you need the right answers already. And if you had them, why would you need the model?
03-check

The way out: checking an answer is much easier than writing one. Think of a sudoku: hard to solve, easy to check. So Good Enough only needs a check. A labelled answer, like a receipt's real total. A test, like code that must pass. Or, with neither, Ultra's own answer, which it then audits.
04-percent

So every percentage here means one thing: on examples the model never saw while tuning, how much it got right by that check. The question is never, is it a hundred? It's: is it as good as Ultra, on the same examples?
05-guards

Three guard rails keep that fair. The test examples are sealed in a Neb-ee-us Sandboxes checkpoint, and every model is marked in its own branch, against the identical key. Ultra runs three times, so we know its own wobble. And a guess check proves that a fixed answer can't pass.
06-tested
We tested it on seven jobs: receipts, bank support, contracts, code, pet photos, video, and a spam filter I uploaded with no answers at all. Plus my own judge bot.
07-demo

Here's the app. Pick receipts, and Good Enough climbs down a ladder of Nemotron models, cheapest first. On each rung, Ultra rewrites the prompt from the tuning examples, the best rewrite is picked on separate validation examples, and only that one is scored on the locked-away receipts. Lightning gets rejected. Nano holds up.
08-prompt

Here's the prompt it handed Nano. Before: a plain description of the job. After: Ultra rewrote it into step-by-step rules, with four worked examples. On the validation receipts, that alone took Nano from eighty-six to ninety percent.
09-squeeze

Then it squeezes. The model is picked, so now it cuts words. Two worked examples instead of four: kept, the score held. No examples, or shorter answers: dropped, the score fell. The result is forty-two times cheaper than Ultra, re-checked on the locked-away receipts.
10-vision

Pictures too. On pet photos, thinking was pure waste: switched off, the same accuracy, six and a half times cheaper, even with smaller photos. On video it's the opposite: thinking off lost thirteen points, so the answer is, keep it on. Same lever, opposite answers. That's why you measure.
11-code

Code was different again. Graded only by unit tests, Nano with thinking on passed eighty-nine percent of a hundred and fifty problems, against Ultra's eighty-five, at twenty-five times cheaper. Ultra's own thinking added nothing.
12-honest
And it says keep Ultra when it should. On contracts, no smaller model held up alone. The best, Lightning, could be eleven points worse.
12b-chain

So we went deeper. Ask two cheap models. If they agree, use their answer. If not, Ultra decides. On contracts, Super and Lightning agreed on three clauses in four. With Ultra settling the rest, the chain matches Ultra, at two and a half times cheaper. Proven the same way, on the locked-away clauses, with no extra model calls.
13-customer

Then I made myself the customer. On my judge bot, the first version said: use Nano, fifteen times cheaper. But a dumb guess, a three on every score, beat every model. That's why the guess check exists: if Ultra can't beat a guess, there's no verdict, and no money spent.
14-own

Bring your own task. I pasted a hundred text messages, with no answers. Ultra wrote the answers and a checker, the checker passed its own test, and Nano does the job seventeen times cheaper. The whole run cost three cents.
14b-audit

And when Ultra writes the answers, it audits itself. A second pass, thinking on, answers every message again. Where the two passes disagree, the message is dropped, not counted. Of the eight it dropped, six were ones it had wrong.
15-impact

For an expense app reading a million receipts a month, that's about forty-four thousand dollars a year, down to about a thousand. Price your mistakes, and it gives the break-even: even in the worst case, Nano wins unless a wrong receipt costs more than seventy-eight cents.
15b-cert
Every run ends with a proof certificate: the setup, the evidence, and the saving, in one link you can share.
16-close
Good Enough. Prove the cheaper model does the job. Open source, and running now on Neb-ee-us Token Factory and Sandboxes.
